claims.text: Superconductivity in uncharacterized high-entropy alloys is chiefly controlled by the average d-electron count, described as the e/a ratio.
Average d-electron count modulates the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the density of states at the Fermi level alter the effectiveness of electron-phonon coupling.
An optimal e/a ratio enhances Cooper pairing and produces a higher superconducting transition temperature.
The proposed starting material is a fully disordered, homogeneous, single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 at.% each.
The proposed starting material does not rely on a Nb-Ta matrix or a Ti-rich configuration.
Small compositional adjustments can shift the average d-electron count while retaining the high-entropy, single-phase structure and keeping every constituent above 5 at.%.
Arc melting followed by homogenization annealing at about 1000°C under argon will ensure complete mixing.
The relevant electronic mediator is the Fermi-level density of states arising from the collective d-electron contribution of the alloying elements.
Disorder-induced band broadening interacts with the collective d-electron contribution in determining the Fermi-level density of states.
Varying average d-electron count alters the Fermi-level density of states, which controls electron-phonon coupling strength.
Maximizing electron-phonon coupling enhances Cooper-pair formation and raises Tc.
Samples whose e/a approaches the proposed optimum will have a higher Tc than the baseline composition.
Tc will decline systematically as e/a moves away from the optimum.
The unmodified baseline has a slightly suboptimal average d-electron count and a moderate Tc.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloys remain disordered and single-phase across the compositional series.
Absence of a systematic correlation or peak in Tc as a function of adjusted e/a would falsify the claim that average d-electron count governs superconductivity.
